title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Summary
-------
This document defines Redwood Inference's canonical architecture and engineering standards for API design, coding, infrastructure (IaC) conventions, model-serving practices, observability, and performance SLOs. It consolidates prior ADRs and provides a lightweight governance and review process for future changes. The goal is consistent cross-team expectations that balance production safety, developer velocity, and inference economics.

Scope
-----
Applies to: all teams implementing public or internal services, model-serving runtime components, infra Terraform modules, and monitoring/alerting prescriptive configs. Exclusions: one-off experimental prototypes may temporarily diverge but must migrate to these standards before merge into mainline or production.

Standards overview (high level)
--------------------------------
- API standards: REST/HTTP first, clear versioning, streaming support, consistent error model, contract stability guarantees.
- Coding standards: language-specific style, linting, typed interfaces, unit/integration test coverage thresholds.
- Infra standards: Terraform modules, tagging, network isolation, secrets management, change-control.
- Model-serving standards: model versioning, quantization profiles, batching and KV cache defaults, fallback policies.
- Observability standards: OTel tracing, structured JSON logs, canonical metrics, dashboards and alerting tiers.
- Performance standards: service-level SLOs, perf-bench baselines, continuous perf regression checks.

API Standards
-------------
Purpose: make services predictable and backwards-compatible for both internal and external clients.

Design principles:
- API-first: public APIs must have an OpenAPI spec checked into the same repo and validated in CI.
- Versioning: use path-based major versioning (/v1/, /v2/). Non-breaking changes can be rolling changes with documented deprecation windows.
- Idempotency: write-mutating endpoints (create/submit) must accept an idempotency-key header and be safe to retry.
- Streaming: support chunked transfer encoding for large/long-running responses. When streaming is provided, also offer a polling/async fallback.
- Error model: standardized JSON error envelope: {
  "error": {"code": "<short_code>", "message": "human readable", "details": [] }
}. Use HTTP status codes per RFC.
- Contract tests: providers must publish and run consumer-driven contract tests in CI.

Required headers and correlation:
- X-Request-ID (generated if absent)
- X-Redwood-Region for routing telemetry (us-west-2, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1)
- Authorization: Bearer for public endpoints; mTLS for internal control-plane endpoints

Rate limiting and quotas:
- Per-customer rate limit buckets enforced at edge gateways. Default hosted-tier throttle: 120 reqs/min per API key. Dedicated customers have configurable limits.

Coding Standards
----------------
Languages: primary services should be implemented in Go (backend infra) or Python (data/ML tooling). Exceptions require RFC and approval.

Basic rules:
- Follow language-specific style guides (gofmt/goimports, black/ruff for Python).
- Static typing where available (Go, typed Python with mypy).
- Linting: ruff (Python), staticcheck (Go) in pre-commit and CI; no new linter warnings allowed on merge.
- Tests: minimum unit coverage 60% for new modules; critical runtime components 80%+. All PRs require unit tests and relevant integration tests.
- CI gate: all checks (lint, test, contract tests) must pass.
- Dependency policy: prefer vetted internal dependency manifest. Security-scan all third-party dependencies via Snyk or internal tooling.
- Secrets: do not commit keys; use HashiCorp Vault or cloud KMS.

Coding conventions for runtime-heavy components:
- Avoid global singletons; prefer interfaces for easier mocking.
- Explicit CPU/GPU concurrency controls documented in config.
- Provide a lightweight dev-mode that can run without GPU.

Infrastructure (IaC) Standards
-----------------------------
- Terraform modules under org-level registry. All infra changes go through PRs that run 'terraform plan' in CI.
- Naming and tagging: resource names must include team, env, service, and short id. Standard tags: Team, Owner, Env, CostCenter, Compliance.
- Network: separate VPCs per environment (dev/staging/prod) with strict egress rules. Private subnetting for model-serving GPU clusters.
- Secrets and keys: use Vault for short-lived credentials; KMS for long-term keys; do not store secrets in plaintext state. Terraform state stored in remote backend with encryption and enforced ACLs.
- Change control: critical infra (network, IAM, KMS) requires approver from Security.
- Billing and capacity: each Dedicated/Private deployment must include cost center and capacity plan file in the module directory.

Model-Serving Standards
-----------------------
Objective: ensure model deployments are safe, reproducible, and performant across hosted, dedicated and private modes.

Versioning and packaging:
- Model artifacts must be versioned (semantic-style model-X.Y.Z) and have a manifest with: model_hash, tokenizer_hash, config, quantization_profile_id, serving_image.
- Immutable bundles stored in S3 with restricted access and audit logging.

Quantization & profiles:
- Quantization profiles stored under /quantization-profiles with metadata: target-hw, expected-rand, supported-seq-lens, accuracy-tolerance.
- Default profiles: fp16 (nvidia-A100), int8-llm-q8 (t4/rtx). Profile selection automated by Optimize service but can be pinned per-customer.

Runtime config (defaults):
- batch_size: adaptive, default max 64 for GPU-pool-1
- max_seq_len: 4096 for long context models, 1024 default for small models
- kv_cache_ttl: 30m for hosted sessions; configurable for Dedicated
- cold_start_grace: pre-warm pools during traffic ramps; prefer warm pools for high-SLO endpoints

Safety & fallbacks:
- All production model endpoints must register a fallback plan (smaller model/smarter batching) and a circuit-breaker policy.
- Canary deployment: 1% traffic for 24h, health-checks, quality-guardrails (eval prompt-set pass/fail).

Model observability:
- Log per-request model metadata: model_name, model_version, quant_profile, seq_len, tokens_generated, latency_ms, truncation_flags.

Observability Standards
----------------------
Principles: instrument early, correlate traces/metrics/logs, provide actionable alerts.

Telemetry stack:
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry (OTel) tracing with deterministic span naming. Sample rate: default 5% for general services, 100% for latency/production-critical model-serving spans for first 30s after a new deployment (ramp sampling).
- Metrics: Prometheus-compatible metrics with exponential histograms for latency. Metric name format: redwood_<service>_<resource>_<metric>. Use labels sparingly: service, env, region, model_name, model_version, shard.
- Logs: structured JSON logs at INFO/WARN/ERROR; include correlation fields (X-Request-ID, trace_id). Avoid PII in logs.

Canonical SLI/SLOs (examples)
- Hosted public-generation endpoints: Availability SLO = 99.95% monthly; Latency SLO p95 < 200ms for short-context text-generation (<=256 tokens), p99 < 500ms.
- Dedicated customer endpoints (committed): Availability SLO = 99.9% with contractual TTR for incidents.
- Embeddings endpoint: p95 < 120ms; throughput target 2k reqs/s per 8-GPU pool at batch sizes tuned per model.

Alerting tiers and thresholds
- Critical (pager): Availability drop below 99.9% per-region sustained for 5m, or p99 latency > 2x SLO for 10m.
- High (email+Slack): p95 latency > 1.5x SLO sustained 15m, or error rate spike (5xx > 0.5%).
- Medium: saturation signals (GPU memory > 85% for 10m).

Dashboards and runbooks
- Every service must publish a per-route dashboard: latency histograms, error rates, CPU/GPU utilization, queue length, KB cache hit rate, and recent deploys.
- Runbooks: link to a single runbook artifact in confluence under eng-platform/runbooks.

Performance Standards
---------------------
Benchmarks and targets:
- Throughput goals: inference runtime should target 10k tokens/s per A100-80GB across well-optimized LLMs at default batching profiles. (Model-dependent and measured via our benchmarking suite.)
- Cold-start: container spin-up and model load should be <90s for large models with pre-warmed images; warm-pool cold-start target <10s.
- Per-GPU concurrency: default 4 concurrent streams per A100 for long-context models; tune per-model in quantization profile.

Performance validation:
- All production model changes must be accompanied by perf-bench results and regression thresholds defined in the PR.
- CI must run lightweight perf smoke tests; full perf suite runs nightly and on major releases.

ADR registry and notable decisions
--------------------------------
We maintain a concise ADR registry as the source of truth for architecture trade-offs. Each ADR is a short Markdown artifact checked into the relevant repo and referenced here. Notable ADRs: 
- ADR-2024-11: Adopt unified REST API with streaming support (rationale: consistent UX and lower cognitive load for SDKs).
- ADR-2025-03: Use OpenTelemetry as canonical tracing standard (rationale: vendor-agnostic and wide ecosystem support).
- ADR-2025-08: Quantization profiles stored centrally and referenced by id (rationale: repeatability across Dedicated and Private).
- ADR-2026-02: Default to idempotency keys for create/submit endpoints (rationale: simplify retries across gateways).

Governance and change process
----------------------------
1. Proposal: author opens a Standards RFC in the architecture repo and creates a draft ADR if the proposal changes existing guarantees.
2. Review: solicit reviewers from impacted teams (owner_team must be set). Allow a 5-business-day comment period for non-urgent changes.
3. Approval: final approver for infra/security changes is Security; product-impacting API changes require Product sign-off.
4. Publication: approved ADRs go into the ADR registry and the canonical confluence page.
5. Enforcement: CI checks and repo-level policy (e.g., required OpenAPI file, lint, SLO metadata) enforce compliance.

Rollout and enforcement
-----------------------
- New standards announced in engineering-all with a migration window.
- Critical services must have a migration plan with owner and milestone dates.
- Non-compliant services get a remediation ticket; severity and timelines depend on risk.

Ownership
---------

Appendices
---------
A. Example OpenAPI checklist:
- /openapi.yaml present in repo root
- CI validation (spectral) passes
- Version bump policy documented
- Contract tests present

B. Sample model manifest (YAML)
---
model_name: gptx-open-13b
model_version: 2026-01-12
model_hash: abcdef0123456789
tokenizer_hash: fedcba9876543210
quant_profile_id: int8-llm-q8-v1
serving_image: registry.redwood.io/serving/gptx-open:2026-01-12
---

C. Example alert definitions (Prometheus-alerts format snippet)
- alert: HighModelLatency
  expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(redwood_model_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, service, model_name)) > 0.2
  for: 10m
  labels: { severity: "critical" }
  annotations: { summary: "p95 latency high for {{ $labels.model_name }}" }

D. Links and references
- ADR registry: /confluence/architecture-and-standards/adr-registry
- Quantization profiles: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles
- Runtime perf suite: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite
- Observability best practices: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/observability-best-practices

Contact and questions
---------------------
For clarifications, open an issue on the architecture repo or ping the owners listed under Ownership.
